title: POC weekly sync - throughput optimization

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-14
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Carlos Vega (Nimbus CTO), Priya Singh (Nimbus ML Eng), Dana Lee (Nimbus Infra), Mike Torres (Nimbus SRE), Olivia Park (Nimbus PM)

Summary:
Quick recap of last week's runs, new microbench results, plan for longer steady-state benchmarks focused on continuous batching and concurrency targets, plus infra checks for VPC/dedicated nodes.

Topics:
- throughput results and charts (SE uploaded CSV)
- continuous batching behavior and optimal batch window
- concurrency targets vs tail-latency
- queuing/backpressure and retry behavior
- KV/prefix cache warmup effects
- next experiments and timeline

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll get started in a sec. Uh, quick roll call, Maya and I from Redwood, and Nimbus team?
[00:10] Carlos Vega: Hey Alex, Carlos here. Priya, Dana, Mike and Olivia on the line too.
[00:15] Alex Chen: Great, thanks. Agenda today is throughput optimization, review the microbench you ran, talk continuous batching and concurrency targets and agree next steps.
[00:25] Maya Patel: I posted the CSV in the shared folder, there's two runs — a short warm up and a 15 minute steady state at target qps. The important bits are the effective batching rate and the observed kv cache hit rate.
[00:38] Priya Singh: Quick note — our production traffic is bursty, we have spikes around marketing events. Typical baseline qps is 120, spiky to 1.2k during promos. Payload sizes average ~420 tokens but some go up to 1.8k.
[00:52] Alex Chen: Good, that helps. For this POC we're trying to balance latency SLO 95th at 350ms and target throughput to reduce token cost.
[01:05] Maya Patel: Right. From the microbench, with continuous batching enabled and a batch window of 20ms we saw ~22% throughput improvement at 4 concurrency, but the tail moved out by about 30ms. At 8 concurrency, throughput gains plateaued and we saw queuing spikes.
[01:23] Carlos Vega: When you say queuing spikes, is that request queue inside Redwood runtime or at our ingress?
[01:29] Maya Patel: Mostly within the runtime when the model execution path is saturated. The runtime will queue up tokens and try to form larger batches; if concurrency is high, batch formation latency and scheduling jitter increase.
[01:42] Mike Torres: We saw a few 500s during the test window, were those related?
[01:46] Maya Patel: The 500s were transient — some requests timed out at the client due to our default retry settings. There's a small number of edge cases when cache warmup + large batches cause a spike in CPU/IO on the host.
[02:00] Dana Lee: On infra side we noticed GPU utilization peaked as expected, but we also saw some host memory pressure when multiple KV caches were being populated concurrently.
[02:11] Priya Singh: Is KV cache prefixing beneficial for our use case? We have repeated system prompts and user context for many sessions.
[02:20] Maya Patel: Yes, prefix/KV caching helps a lot for repeated prefixes; hit ratio in the bench was 62% after 3 minutes. That reduced repeated compute and improved tokens/sec. But the warmup period can exacerbate tail latencies.
[02:35] Alex Chen: So tradeoff: aggressive batching + high concurrency improves aggregate throughput and lowers cost, but if your traffic is bursty and tail-latency SLOs are tight, dedicated nodes or a lower concurrency cap with faster batch windows might be better.
[02:52] Carlos Vega: We need predictable 95th percentile under marketing spikes, so even if cost is slightly higher we prefer predictable latency. Does Redwood have burst queues or fallback routing?
[03:03] Alex Chen: Yes — we can route to a higher-priority pool or fallback to a slightly smaller model variant. For Dedicated we can reserve capacity and set concurrency caps per node to reduce queuing jitter. Also there are burst capacity policies to absorb sudden load.
[03:18] Olivia Park: Is there an easy knob to cap the batch window? We prefer low latencies for small requests but still want batching for cost.
[03:25] Maya Patel: We expose batch_window_ms and a target_batch_size. You can set target_batch_size low for short messages and smaller batch_window_ms — that gives predictable latency but reduces batching efficiency. There's also adaptive batching which tries to hit a latency target.
[03:39] Priya Singh: In the microbench you used 20ms window. Can you try 10ms for small payloads and 40ms for larger ones?
[03:45] Maya Patel: Yes we can. The plan we propose: run a steady-state long-run at both concurrency 4 and 8 with batch windows 10/20/40ms and collect tail-latency, batch size distribution, and KV hit rates.
[03:58] Mike Torres: For the record, our SLOs are P95 < 350ms, P99 < 700ms. If any config violates P95 under simulated promo bursts we mark it unacceptable.
[04:10] Alex Chen: Good to know. Also Dana, you mentioned host memory pressure — did you see this consistently or only during cache population?
[04:17] Dana Lee: Mostly during the initial warmup when several sessions hit new prefixes. It stabilized after a few minutes but with high concurrency there are repeated cache evictions and some swap churn.
[04:29] Maya Patel: One mitigation is using quantized model variants and smaller KV cache retention for the POC. That lowers memory but slightly increases compute. Tradeoffs again.
[04:41] Priya Singh: Can Redwood show the estimated token cost delta for the quantized vs full model?
[04:47] Alex Chen: Yes we'll include cost delta in the next summary — quantization typically reduces VM memory and sometimes increases decode latency; cost per token often improves but we'll quantify with your traffic profile.
[04:58] Carlos Vega: Regarding dedicated nodes, what's the minimum you recommend to hit our baseline 1.2k spike capacity predictably?
[05:07] Maya Patel: Rough estimate: two m40-dedicated nodes with 8 concurrent slots each would likely cover baseline with room for bursts, but we'll validate with the long-run benchmark. We'll send a sizing estimate with pricing.
[05:20] Alex Chen: Okay, let's walk through the CSV quickly — Maya, can you highlight the interesting columns?
[05:25] Maya Patel: Sure. There's timestamp, latency_ms, batch_size, kv_hit, gpu_util, and concurrency_slot. Look at the batch_size histogram column — most batches were between 3-6 tokens per batch in steady state. kv_hit went from 12% to 62% after warmup. Latency P95 was about 310ms for 4 concurrency, and 380ms for 8 concurrency on that short run.
[05:48] Priya Singh: So 8 concurrency broke our P95. For marketing spikes that's concerning.
[05:53] Maya Patel: Right. But if we drop batch window to 10ms at 8 concurrency, P95 tightened to 330ms in a quick test, though throughput dipped ~8%.
[06:05] Olivia Park: So we have knobs: reduce concurrency cap, lower batch window, or go dedicated. Which one gives us predictable performance fastest?
[06:13] Alex Chen: The fastest is capping concurrency and tuning batch window; dedicated nodes gives predictability at scale but requires procurement lead time.
[06:21] Carlos Vega: Procurement lead time is our issue — we'd prefer Redwood to help with a short-term dedicated pilot if needed.
[06:28] Alex Chen: We can propose a 2-week dedicated trial with credits; I'll include that in pricing.
[06:35] Mike Torres: Also need to test retry behavior — what happens when requests time out and clients retry, creating thundering herd.
[06:42] Maya Patel: We recommend exponential backoff jitter and client-side concurrency limits. On the runtime we have queue-length throttles and can return 429s rather than letting things pile up. We can simulate those retry patterns in the next benchmark.
[06:55] Priya Singh: Can Redwood instrument and share per-request trace IDs so we can map retries in our logs?
[07:01] Alex Chen: Yes, we'll include trace hooks and the header propagation pattern in the integration notes.
[07:07] Dana Lee: For VPC peering, we have an upcoming change window on 2026-01-19; if Redwood can align the dedicated test then that's best.
[07:15] Alex Chen: We'll try to align. I'll note that as an action item.
[07:19] Maya Patel: Back to batching, one thing to watch is bursty small requests — a small batch_window helps, but if many small requests arrive simultaneously you still get micro-jitters. We can configure a fast path for single-request low-latency mode that bypasses large-batch queues for requests under a threshold.
[07:36] Carlos Vega: That might be useful — many of our customer-facing prompts are under 200 tokens.
[07:41] Priya Singh: For the KV tests, we'll send a sample of repeated user contexts and system prompts that represent 60% of sessions. That should show cache hit behaviour accurately.
[07:51] Maya Patel: Perfect. We'll run KV warmup tests then.
[07:55] Alex Chen: Any other outstanding tech blockers?
[07:58] Mike Torres: We need to confirm k8s egress and firewall rules for peering test — I'll add that to action items as well.
[08:05] Dana Lee: Yep, I'll coordinate with our network team.
[08:08] Alex Chen: Great. Quick recap of decisions: SE to run long-run benchmarks at concurrency 4 and 8 with batch windows 10/20/40ms; include KV warmup runs; simulate retry/backoff patterns; Redwood to send dedicated node sizing and pricing; customer to share traffic profile and prefix sample; align dedicated trial with peering window.
[08:30] Olivia Park: Sounds good. For visibility can you include the per-run graphs (P95/P99, batch size hist, kv hit rate) in the results?
[08:37] Maya Patel: Yes we'll post graphs and the raw CSV.
[08:40] Alex Chen: Okay, we'll wrap up. Any final questions?
[08:43] Priya Singh: One last thing — can you include the cost delta for quantized vs non-quantized in the summary?
[08:48] Alex Chen: Yes, noted.
[08:50] Carlos Vega: Thanks all.
[08:52] Alex Chen: Thanks team, we'll follow up with action items and schedule the deep dive if needed.

End of transcript.
